stories.headline: Why there has never been any lead in a pencil
stories.summary: The black core of a pencil is graphite and has never contained the element lead. In 1565 a large deposit of graphite was discovered at Borrowdale in Cumbria; in 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté found a way to mix powdered graphite with clay and fire the rods in a kiln, and on 30 March 1858 Hymen Lipman received the first patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil.

stories.headline: Every tile in the box: the arithmetic of a domino set
stories.summary: The traditional European domino set consists of 28 tiles, also known as bones, stones or simply dominoes, featuring every combination of spot counts from zero to six. Larger sets extend the idea: a double-nine set has 55 tiles and a double-twelve set 91.

stories.headline: The hill where the world's clocks are set
stories.summary: The Royal Observatory, Greenwich, stands on a hill in Greenwich Park in south-east London, overlooking the River Thames. It was commissioned by King Charles II in 1675, and because the Prime Meridian passed through it, it gave its name to Greenwich Mean Time. The meridian was adopted as the world's Prime Meridian at the International Meridian Conference in Washington on 22 October 1884.
